growth_story.headline: The Cayman Islands' income per person fell hard after 2007 and has climbed back slowly since 2015, but in 2024 it was still 12.3 percent below its 2007 peak.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in the Cayman Islands peaked in 2007 and then fell for most of the next seven years: from 2007 to 2014 it shrank by 2.8 percent a year, with the deepest drop, 9.8 percent, in 2009. The Caribbean Development Bank traces that slump to the global financial crisis, which hit the islands' financial sector hard, and it counted Cayman among the few economies in the region where output fell by more than 5 percent in 2009. From 2015 to 2024 growth turned positive, at 1.1 percent a year; for the early years of that recovery the bank credits a boom in tourism and a shift towards professional, scientific and technical services, while finance returned to modest growth. The pandemic broke the recovery in 2020, when income per person fell 6.8 percent, but as tourism reopened growth ran at between 2.7 and 3.7 percent a year from 2021 to 2023. Even so, income per person in 2024 was still 12.3 percent below its 2007 peak, and lower than in 2006, the first year of the record.

threads.text: The 2008-09 global crisis hit the Cayman Islands' financial sector hard. Output fell harder in 2009 than in most of the region, and finance's direct share of the economy was smaller in 2016 than in 2007.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe recoveries that look stronger than the income per person record. The Caribbean Development Bank said growth after the crisis came close to pre-crisis rates, yet income per person grew only 0.4 to 0.9 percent a year in 2015-2017. It also reported that output passed its 2019 level in 2022, while income per person stayed below its 2019 level until 2023. The bank's reports of fast population growth from rising work permits point to the gap: total output grew, but it was shared among more people.
